cards.definition_en: The rule of giving every user or program only the permissions that it needs for its task, and nothing more.
examples: Following least privilege, the report tool can read the data but not change it.
Under least privilege a support agent cannot see payment details.
common_mistakes: Giving everyone administrator rights to avoid support requests.
Thinking it is a one-time setting: permissions should be reviewed regularly.

cards.definition_en: A way of managing permissions in which rights are attached to roles, and people get rights by being given a role.
examples: With role-based access control a new accountant only needs the accountant role.
The number of roles in role-based access control tends to grow over time.
common_mistakes: Giving permissions to individual users directly while calling it role-based.
Creating one role for every person.

cards.definition_en: Checking a person's identity with two or more different kinds of proof, such as a password plus a code from a phone.
examples: Multi-factor authentication stopped the attacker who had a stolen password.
The bank asks for multi-factor authentication when you log in from a new device.
common_mistakes: Counting two passwords as two factors: they are the same kind of proof.
Thinking it makes a weak password unimportant.

cards.definition_en: A setup where a person logs in once and can then use several separate applications without logging in again.
examples: Thanks to single sign-on, staff use one account for mail, chat and the wiki.
If the single sign-on account is stolen, every connected application is at risk.
common_mistakes: Using one shared password for many services and calling it single sign-on.
Writing 'single sign-in'; the usual term is 'sign-on'.

cards.definition_en: A standard that lets an application get limited access to a user's data on another service without receiving the user's password.
examples: The calendar app uses OAuth to read your events without knowing your password.
Each OAuth scope describes what the application may do.
common_mistakes: Treating OAuth as a way to log users in: it is about authorization, not identity.
Writing it as 'O-Auth' or 'Oauth'.

cards.definition_en: A layer on top of OAuth that lets an application find out who the user is after they log in at an identity provider.
examples: The site lets you sign in with OpenID Connect through your company account.
OpenID Connect adds an identity token to the OAuth flow.
common_mistakes: Mixing it up with OAuth: OAuth grants access, OpenID Connect proves identity.
Confusing it with the old OpenID standard.

cards.definition_en: An XML-based standard for passing login and permission information between an identity provider and an application, common in company single sign-on.
examples: The university portal logs students in with SAML.
The SAML assertion tells the application who the user is and for how long.
common_mistakes: Thinking SAML is mainly for mobile apps: it is typical for web single sign-on.
Pronouncing every letter separately: it is usually said as a word.

cards.definition_en: A short-lived credential that an application shows to an API to prove it has permission to act.
examples: The API rejected the request because the access token had expired.
A stolen access token is dangerous only until it expires.
common_mistakes: Storing an access token in a public repository.
Giving access tokens a lifetime of many months.

cards.definition_en: A long-lived credential that lets an application obtain new access tokens without asking the user to log in again.
examples: The app quietly gets a new access token with its refresh token.
Refresh token rotation makes a stolen token useless after the next use.
common_mistakes: Sending the refresh token to the API with every request.
Confusing it with an access token.

cards.definition_en: A compact token that carries information such as a user identifier and an expiry time in JSON, protected by a signature that the server can check.
examples: The server checks the signature of the JSON Web Token before trusting its claims.
A JSON Web Token is easy to read, so it must not contain secrets.
common_mistakes: Assuming the content is encrypted: it is only encoded and signed.
Accepting a token without checking the signature and the expiry.

cards.definition_en: A set of rules about passwords, such as minimum length, checks against known leaked passwords and what to do after a leak.
examples: Our password policy requires at least twelve characters.
A good password policy helps people choose long passphrases instead of tricks.
common_mistakes: Forcing frequent changes, which often leads to weaker passwords.
Writing the rules only for users and not checking them on the server.

cards.definition_en: An attack that tries a very large number of passwords or keys one after another until one works.
collocations: brute-force attack on a login page
examples: Rate limiting makes a brute-force attack on the login form slow and noisy.
A short password falls quickly to a brute-force attack.
common_mistakes: Thinking it needs cleverness: it simply tries many guesses.
Mixing it up with credential stuffing, which uses real leaked pairs.

cards.definition_en: An attack that tries username and password pairs leaked from one service on many other services, hoping people reused them.
examples: Credential stuffing succeeded because many customers reused the same password.
Multi-factor authentication blocks most credential stuffing attempts.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with a brute-force attack: here the passwords are not guessed.
Writing 'credentials stuffing'.

cards.definition_en: Gaining more rights than one was meant to have, for example when an ordinary user becomes an administrator.
examples: A bug in the service allowed privilege escalation from a normal account to root.
Patching the kernel closed the privilege escalation hole.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with lateral movement, which means moving to other machines without gaining higher rights.
Thinking it always requires physical access.

cards.definition_en: A service that stores users' accounts and confirms who they are for other applications.
examples: The app trusts the identity provider to check the user's password.
When the identity provider is down, nobody can log in.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with the application that the user wants to use.
Writing 'identification provider'.

cards.definition_en: A list attached to a resource that says which users or systems may do what with it.
examples: An access control list on the folder allows only the finance team to read the files.
Each entry in the access control list names a user and a permission.
common_mistakes: Leaving the default entry that allows everyone.
Thinking the list controls who can log in: it controls access to a specific resource.

cards.definition_en: Temporarily blocking an account after several wrong password attempts, to slow down guessing.
examples: Account lockout stops an attacker from trying thousands of passwords.
A strict account lockout can be abused to block real users.
common_mistakes: Locking the account forever instead of for a limited time.
Ignoring that attackers can lock other people's accounts on purpose.

cards.definition_en: A password-free login method based on a key pair stored on the user's device and unlocked with a fingerprint, face or device code.
examples: With a passkey you unlock the login with your fingerprint instead of typing a password.
A passkey cannot be handed over to a fake website.
common_mistakes: Thinking a passkey is a long password.
Believing the fingerprint itself is sent to the website.

cards.definition_en: Splitting an important task between several people so that nobody can complete a risky action alone.
examples: Separation of duties means one person writes the payment and another approves it.
The audit found a lack of separation of duties in the accounting team.
common_mistakes: Dividing work only for convenience, without any control purpose.
Giving two people the same account.

cards.definition_en: A time-ordered record of who did what in a system and when it happened.
examples: The audit log showed that the file was deleted at midnight.
Administrators must not be able to edit the audit log.
common_mistakes: Storing the audit log only on the server that may be attacked.
Recording actions without the user and the time.

cards.definition_en: The automatic end of a login session after a period of inactivity or after a maximum time.
examples: The banking site applies a short session timeout for safety.
After the session timeout the user has to log in again.
common_mistakes: Setting a session timeout of several weeks for a sensitive application.
Ending the session only in the browser and not on the server.

cards.definition_en: Identification based on body features such as fingerprints, the face or the voice.
examples: The phone unlocks with biometrics instead of a code.
Biometrics cannot be changed if they leak, unlike a password.
common_mistakes: Writing 'biometry' for the technology: the usual word is 'biometrics'.
Thinking biometrics are secret like passwords.

cards.definition_en: A password that works only for a single login or for a very short time.
examples: The bank sends a one-time password by text message.
A one-time password expires after thirty seconds.
common_mistakes: Reusing a one-time password.
Sharing the code with a caller who claims to be from support.

cards.definition_en: An arrangement in which several organizations trust each other's login systems, so a user can access different services with one identity.
examples: Federation lets visiting researchers use their home university account.
The federation depends on trust between the identity providers.
common_mistakes: Using it only for countries: in IT it also names a trust arrangement between systems.
Confusing it with single sign-on inside one organization.

cards.definition_en: A security approach that does not trust a request just because it comes from the internal network, and checks every user and device each time.
examples: Under zero trust, even a laptop in the office must prove who it is.
Zero trust assumes that an attacker may already be inside.
common_mistakes: Thinking it is a product that can be bought and switched on.
Trusting everything inside the company network.
